title: Ὁπλισμὸς Πατρόκλου
titleEn: The Ship Afire and the Myrmidons Armed — Iliad 16.101–209
part: The Ship Afire and the Myrmidons Armed (16.101–209)
about: Ajax, worn out and hard pressed by shafts, holds his ground until Hector cuts the head from his spear; he sees that Zeus is giving the Trojans the day and gives way, and they throw fire on a ship. The poet calls on the Muses, and Achilles, seeing the flames, strikes his thighs and tells Patroclus to arm while he gathers the people. Patroclus puts on Achilles’ greaves, breastplate, sword, shield and helmet and takes two spears, but leaves Achilles’ great ash-spear, which no one else can swing. Automedon yokes the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius, with the mortal Pedasus beside them. Achilles arms the Myrmidons, who are likened to wolves gorging on a kill, and the poet names the five leaders of their five ranks, telling how Menesthius and Eudorus were born. Achilles draws them up and tells them to remember how they blamed him for keeping them from the war: now the fighting they longed for is here, and let each man fight.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
Αἴας δ’ οὐκ ἔτ’ ἔμιμνε·
sentences.l:
So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking,
but Ajax no longer remained;
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another, but Ajax no longer held his ground;
sentences.n: The scene cuts from Achilles and Patroclus, the ‘they’ of οἳ μέν (οἵ is the article used as a pronoun), to the fighting at the ships, and μέν … δέ sets what they said against what Ajax did. Line 101 also stands at 5.274, where it opens a different scene; here it is only a bridge. ἀγόρευον and ἔμιμνε are imperfects with no augment (Attic ἠγόρευον, ἔμενε), and μίμνω is the reduplicated present of μένω ‘stay, stand fast’. Αἴας is Telamonian Ajax, named in full at line 116.

sentences.t: βιάζετο γὰρ βελέεσσι·
sentences.l: for he was being pressed hard by shafts;
sentences.i: for he was hard pressed by shafts;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason he can no longer stand. βιάζετο is the passive of βιάζω ‘press hard, force’, and βελέεσσι is the epic dative plural of βέλος ‘shaft’, the word for any missile thrown or shot. The unit is short because two ano teleiai fall in line 102, one after ἔμιμνε and one after βελέεσσι.

sentences.t:
δάμνα μιν Ζηνός τε νόος καὶ Τρῶες ἀγαυοὶ
βάλλοντες·
sentences.l:
Were subduing him both the mind of Zeus and the Trojans, noble ones,
striking him;
sentences.i: both the mind of Zeus and the noble Trojans, striking him, were overcoming him;
sentences.n: δάμνα is an imperfect with no augment (ἐδάμνα) of δάμνημι, the older form of δαμάζω ‘subdue, overcome’, and it has two subjects: Ζηνός … νόος ‘the mind of Zeus’ and the Trojans, who are named after it (Ζηνός is the genitive from the older stem Ζην-). Setting the mind of Zeus beside the Trojans makes it a force on Ajax as real as their shafts. ἀγαυοί ‘noble’ is a stock epithet of the Trojans, translated every time; βάλλοντες ‘striking’ hangs on Τρῶες.

sentences.t:
δεινὴν δὲ περὶ κροτάφοισι φαεινὴ
πήληξ βαλλομένη καναχὴν ἔχε, βάλλετο δ’ αἰεὶ
κὰπ φάλαρ’ εὐποίηθ’·
sentences.i: and about his temples the shining helmet, as it was struck, kept up a fearsome clang, and it was always being struck down along its well-made plates;
sentences.n: The subject of ἔχε and of βάλλετο is the helmet, πήληξ, with φαεινή ‘shining’. δεινήν agrees with καναχήν ‘clang’, which stands in the next line, and ἔχε is ‘kept up’; κροτάφοισι is ‘temples’ in the epic dative plural -οισι. In the last clause κὰπ is κατά (before φ) with the accusative φάλαρα, ‘down along the plates’; βάλλετο is the plain verb, so there is no tmesis here. φάλαρα are some metal pieces of the helmet; whether bosses or cheek-plates is not known, and ‘plates’ is a guess. εὐποίηθ’ is εὐποίητα ‘well-made’ with its last vowel elided and τ made θ before the rough breathing of ὅ.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀριστερὸν ὦμον ἔκαμνεν
ἔμπεδον αἰὲν ἔχων σάκος αἰόλον·
sentences.l:
And he, in the left shoulder, was growing weary,
steadily always holding the glancing shield;
sentences.i: and he was growing weary in his left shoulder, always holding the glancing shield steadily;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ, with ὁ as a pronoun, turns back to Ajax. ἀριστερὸν ὦμον is an accusative of respect, ‘in respect of the left shoulder’, with ἔκαμνεν, the imperfect of κάμνω ‘grow weary, toil’; the shoulder that tires is the one under the shield. ἔμπεδον ‘steadily’ and αἰέν ‘always’ (the same word as αἰεί, Attic ἀεί) both go with ἔχων ‘holding’. σάκος αἰόλον ‘glancing shield’ is a standing phrase; αἰόλος is ‘quick-moving, glinting’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ δύναντο
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ πελεμίξαι ἐρείδοντες βελέεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and they could not
about him shake him, pressing hard with shafts.
sentences.i: and they could not shake him, pressing hard about him with their shafts.
sentences.n: The Trojans are still the subject. δύναντο is an imperfect with no augment (Attic ἐδύναντο). πελεμίξαι is the aorist infinitive of πελεμίζω ‘shake, make reel’, and the Greek gives it no object: ‘him’ is understood from αὐτῷ, which with ἀμφί means ‘about him’. ἐρείδοντες ‘pressing hard’ is the active participle of ἐρείδω.

sentences.t:
αἰεὶ δ’ ἀργαλέῳ ἔχετ’ ἄσθματι, κὰδ δέ οἱ ἱδρὼς
πάντοθεν ἐκ μελέων πολὺς ἔρρεεν, οὐδέ πῃ εἶχεν
ἀμπνεῦσαι·
sentences.i: He was always in the grip of grievous panting, and sweat in abundance ran down from his limbs on every side, and in no way could he recover his breath;
sentences.n: ἔχετο is the imperfect passive of ἔχω ‘was held’, with the dative ἀργαλέῳ ἄσθματι ‘grievous panting’. κὰδ … ἔρρεεν is a tmesis, κατέρρεεν ‘ran down’, with κὰδ = κατά before δ; οἱ is ‘on him’, and πάντοθεν ‘from all sides’ has the suffix -θεν for ‘from’. ἔρρεεν is the imperfect of ῥέω, uncontracted. πῃ is an enclitic ‘in any way’. εἶχεν with an infinitive means ‘was able’, and ἀμπνεῦσαι is ἀναπνεῦσαι ‘to draw breath again’, with ἀν- changed to ἀμ- before π.

sentences.t: πάντῃ δὲ κακὸν κακῷ ἐστήρικτο.
sentences.l: and on every side evil upon evil had been fixed.
sentences.i: and on every side evil had been set fast upon evil.
sentences.n: ἐστήρικτο is the pluperfect passive of στηρίζω ‘prop, set firm’: evil is pictured as built up, one thing fixed on another. κακόν is ‘evil’, the plain word for hardship, here the shafts and his exhaustion together. πάντῃ ‘on every side’.

sentences.t:
ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι,
ὅππως δὴ πρῶτον πῦρ ἔμπεσε νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
Tell now to me, Muses, who hold the Olympian halls,
how indeed first fire fell upon the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Tell me now, Muses, you who hold the halls of Olympus, how it was that fire first fell upon the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The poet stops the narrative to call on the Muses for what comes next. ἔσπετε is the aorist imperative of ἐννέπω ‘tell’, and Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι ‘who hold the Olympian halls’ is a stock phrase, found before at 2.484. ὅππως is ὅπως ‘how’, introducing an indirect question, and δή adds ‘indeed’. ἔμπεσε is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’ with no augment, and νηυσίν is the epic dative plural of ναῦς.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ Αἴαντος δόρυ μείλινον ἄγχι παραστὰς
πλῆξ’ ἄορι μεγάλῳ αἰχμῆς παρὰ καυλὸν ὄπισθεν,
ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἀπάραξε·
sentences.i: Standing close beside Ajax, Hector struck his ashen spear with his great sword, by the socket of the spearhead, behind it, and cut it right through;
sentences.n: Ἕκτωρ is the subject of πλῆξ’ (πλῆξε, aorist of πλήσσω ‘strike’), with Αἴαντος δόρυ μείλινον ‘Ajax’s ashen spear’ as its object, and ἄγχι παραστάς ‘standing close by’ is an aorist participle. ἄορι ‘with a sword’ is a second word for the weapon the poem usually calls ξίφος. αἰχμῆς παρὰ καυλόν is ‘beside the socket of the point’: αἰχμή is the spearhead and καυλός means ‘stem’, here the socket where the head meets the shaft, and ὄπισθεν ‘behind’ says the blow fell behind the head. ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ goes with ἀπάραξε, the aorist of ἀπαράσσω ‘strike off’.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν Τελαμώνιος Αἴας
πῆλ’ αὔτως ἐν χειρὶ κόλον δόρυ, τῆλε δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ
αἰχμὴ χαλκείη χαμάδις βόμβησε πεσοῦσα.
sentences.l:
this, on the one hand, Telamonian Ajax
swung just so in his hand, a docked spear, and far from him
the bronze point boomed, falling to the ground.
sentences.i: Telamonian Ajax swung the docked spear in his hand to no purpose, and far from him the bronze point boomed as it fell to the ground.
sentences.n: τὸ μέν ‘this one’ is the shaft Ajax is left holding, picked up again as κόλον δόρυ ‘the docked spear’ (κόλος means cut short); the point is the other half, αἰχμὴ χαλκείη ‘the bronze point’. πῆλ’ is πῆλε, aorist of πάλλω ‘swing’, and αὔτως ‘just so’ carries the sense of doing a thing to no purpose. τῆλε ‘far’ goes with ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘from him’ (αὐτοῦ could also be the spear, ‘from it’). χαμάδις is ‘to the ground’, βόμβησε ‘boomed’, and πεσοῦσα is an aorist participle of πίπτω. Τελαμώνιος tells this Ajax from the other.

sentences.t:
γνῶ δ’ Αἴας κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονα ῥίγησέν τε
ἔργα θεῶν, ὅ ῥα πάγχυ μάχης ἐπὶ μήδεα κεῖρε
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης, Τρώεσσι δὲ βούλετο νίκην·
sentences.i: And Ajax knew in his blameless heart, and shuddered at the works of the gods: that Zeus who thunders on high was cutting short the counsels of battle altogether, and wanted victory for the Trojans.
sentences.n: γνῶ (ἔγνω, ‘recognised’) and ῥίγησε ‘shuddered’ share the object ἔργα θεῶν ‘the works of the gods’, which the clause with ὅ spells out; ὅ is the neuter ‘that’ (the fact that). ἐπὶ … κεῖρε is a tmesis for ἐπέκειρε, from ἐπικείρω ‘cut off, cut short’; μήδεα μάχης ‘the counsels of battle’ are not said to be anyone’s, and the picture is of Zeus breaking off the plans that would hold the fight. ὑψιβρεμέτης ‘who thunders on high’ is a stock epithet of Zeus, translated every time. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known; ‘blameless’ is the traditional rendering. Τρώεσσι is ‘for the Trojans’.

sentences.t: χάζετο δ’ ἐκ βελέων.
sentences.l: And he gave ground out of the shafts.
sentences.i: He gave ground, out of the reach of the shafts.
sentences.n: χάζετο is the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘give ground, draw back’. ἐκ βελέων ‘out of the shafts’ means out of the range of the missiles, and the English adds ‘reach’ to say so. The sentence ends at the full stop, and it is Ajax’s yielding that leaves the ship open to the fire.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἔμβαλον ἀκάματον πῦρ
νηῒ θοῇ·
sentences.l:
And they threw an untiring fire
upon the swift ship;
sentences.i: And they threw untiring fire upon the swift ship;
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the article used as ‘they’: the Trojans. ἔμβαλον is the aorist of ἐμβάλλω ‘throw on’. ἀκάματον πῦρ ‘untiring fire’ is a stock phrase, translated the same way every time; ἀκάματος is ‘not tiring’, a fire that does not die down. νηῒ θοῇ ‘upon the swift ship’ is a dative singular, the diaeresis on νηῒ marking its two syllables; the ship is not named.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ αἶψα κατ’ ἀσβέστη κέχυτο φλόξ.
sentences.l: and over it at once unquenchable had been poured flame.
sentences.i: and at once a flame that would never go out spread over it.
sentences.n: τῆς is the ship in the genitive, governed by κατά; κατ’ … κέχυτο is a tmesis for κατεκέχυτο, the pluperfect passive of καταχέω ‘pour down over’, which makes the fire spread like a liquid. The pluperfect says the flame was already poured out. ἀσβέστη (ἄσβεστος ‘unquenchable’, that cannot be put out) agrees with φλόξ ‘flame’, and αἶψα is ‘at once’.

sentences.t: ὣς τὴν μὲν πρυμνὴν πῦρ ἄμφεπεν·
sentences.l: So her stern the fire was busy about;
sentences.i: So the fire was busy about her stern;
sentences.n: ὣς … μέν rounds off the burning, and the αὐτάρ of the next clause answers the μέν. τήν is the ship, with πρυμνήν ‘stern’ as the part the fire has caught. ἄμφεπεν is the imperfect of ἀμφέπω ‘be busy about’, a word for a person tending something, here said of fire as if it were at work.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
μηρὼ πληξάμενος Πατροκλῆα προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
but Achilles,
striking both thighs, addressed Patroclus:
sentences.i: but Achilles struck both his thighs and said to Patroclus:
sentences.n: αὐτάρ answers the μέν of the clause before, taking the story from the fire to Achilles, who is watching. μηρώ is the dual ‘the two thighs’ and πληξάμενος the aorist middle participle of πλήσσω, ‘having struck his own’, a gesture of strong feeling. Πατροκλῆα is the epic accusative of Πάτροκλος. προσέειπεν is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’; it leads into the speech that follows.

sentences.t: ὄρσεο διογενὲς Πατρόκλεες ἱπποκέλευθε·
sentences.l: “Rise up, Zeus-sprung Patroclus, horse-urging one;
sentences.i: “Rouse yourself, Zeus-born Patroclus, you who urge horses on;
sentences.n: ὄρσεο is the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with the epic ending -σεο (Attic -σαι). διογενές ‘Zeus-born’ is a stock form of address. ἱπποκέλευθε is the vocative of an epithet of Patroclus built on ἵππος ‘horse’ and κέλευθος ‘way’; whether it means ‘who drives his horses along the way’ or comes from the root of κελεύω ‘urge’ is not certain, and ‘who urges horses on’ is the likely sense. The speech begins here and Achilles speaks to the end of line 129.

sentences.t: λεύσσω δὴ παρὰ νηυσὶ πυρὸς δηΐοιο ἰωήν·
sentences.l: I see now beside the ships the roar of hostile fire;
sentences.i: I see now, beside the ships, the roar of hostile fire;
sentences.n: λεύσσω is ‘I look upon, I see’, and δή adds ‘now’. ἰωή is properly a cry or sound, so ‘see the roar’ is a loose, almost mixed phrase: he sees the blaze and hears it. πυρὸς δηΐοιο ‘hostile fire’ stands also at 2.415; δηΐοιο is the epic genitive of δήϊος ‘hostile’. νηυσί is the epic dative plural, with παρά ‘beside’.

sentences.t: μὴ δὴ νῆας ἕλωσι καὶ οὐκέτι φυκτὰ πέλωνται·
sentences.l: lest indeed they take the ships, and no more escapable things come to be;
sentences.i: lest they take the ships, and there be no more way of escape.
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctive ἕλωσι (αἱρέω ‘take’) is the fear clause ‘lest they take’, and πέλωνται, the subjunctive of πέλομαι ‘come to be’, continues it. φυκτά is the neuter plural of a verbal adjective of φεύγω, ‘things to be escaped, escapable’, and the Greek leaves it there: ‘a way of escape’ is the sense the context gives. οὐκέτι is ‘no longer’, δή adds urgency.

sentences.t: δύσεο τεύχεα θᾶσσον, ἐγὼ δέ κε λαὸν ἀγείρω.
sentences.l: Put on your armour more quickly, and I shall gather the people.”
sentences.i: Put your armour on quickly, and I shall gather the people.”
sentences.n: δύσεο is the aorist imperative middle of δύω ‘go into’, which with the accusative τεύχεα ‘armour’ means ‘put on’; -σεο is the epic ending for Attic -σαι. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς ‘swift’ used as a command to hurry, ‘the quicker the better’. ἐγὼ δέ κε … ἀγείρω is κε with a short-vowel subjunctive, which gives ‘I shall’. λαόν is ‘the people’, here the Myrmidons, whom he arms next. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, Πάτροκλος δὲ κορύσσετο νώροπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Patroclus armed himself in flashing bronze.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Patroclus armed himself in flashing bronze.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech (φάτο is the unaugmented imperfect middle of φημί (ἔφατο)), and a typical arming scene follows: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet, spears, in the order of Paris’ arming at 3.330–338, and lines 131–132 and 135–138 are Paris’ own, with 139 nearly so. κορύσσετο is the imperfect middle of κορύσσω ‘arm’. νώροπι χαλκῷ ‘flashing bronze’ is a stock phrase in the dative; the sense of νώροψ is not known, and ‘flashing’ is the traditional guess.

sentences.t:
κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε
καλάς, ἀργυρέοισιν ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας·
sentences.l:
Greaves first about his shins he set,
fine ones, with silver ankle-clasps fitted;
sentences.i: First he set fine greaves about his shins, fitted with silver ankle-clasps;
sentences.n: These two lines are also 3.330–331, Paris putting on his greaves, and they take the same English. κνημῖδες ‘greaves’ are the shin-guards; ἐπισφυρίοις (ἐπί + σφυρόν ‘ankle’) are the ankle-clasps that fasten them. ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, agreeing with κνημῖδας ‘fitted’, and καλάς ‘fine’ stands at the start of the second line, parted from its noun by the line division. περί with the dative κνήμῃσιν is ‘about his shins’ (κνήμῃσιν is the epic dative plural). ἔθηκε is ‘set, put on’.

sentences.t:
δεύτερον αὖ θώρηκα περὶ στήθεσσιν ἔδυνε
ποικίλον ἀστερόεντα ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο.
sentences.l:
Second, in turn, a breastplate about his chest he put on,
intricate, starry, of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.i: Second, he put on about his chest the intricate, starry breastplate of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus.
sentences.n: Line 133 also stands at 11.19 with a different second line, and its wording is kept as far as this sentence allows. θώρηκα is the accusative of θώραξ ‘breastplate’, and ἔδυνε the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’ (a form of δύω). ποικίλον ‘intricate’ and ἀστερόεντα ‘starry’ agree with θώρηκα; the word does not say what makes it starry, whether studs or inlay. The genitive ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο ‘of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus’ names Achilles, and so the breastplate is his: the first sign that Patroclus is arming in Achilles’ armour.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
χάλκεον, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε·
sentences.l:
and about his shoulders he slung the silver-studded sword,
bronze, and then the shield, great and stout;
sentences.i: and slung about his shoulders the silver-studded sword, a bronze one, and then the shield, great and stout;
sentences.n: These lines are also 3.334–335 and take the same English. ἀμφὶ … βάλετο is ‘slung about himself’, ἀμφί standing apart from the aorist middle of βάλλω, and ὤμοισιν is the epic dative plural ‘on the shoulders’. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον ‘the silver-studded sword’ is a stock phrase, and χάλκεον ‘bronze’ begins the second line as a description added after the noun. σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε is ‘the shield, great and stout’.

sentences.t:
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἰφθίμῳ κυνέην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκεν
ἵππουριν· δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν.
sentences.l:
and on his mighty head the well-made helmet he placed,
horse-tailed, and fearsomely the crest above nodded;
sentences.i: and on his mighty head he placed the well-made helmet, with its horsetail plume, and fearsomely the crest nodded above;
sentences.n: These lines are also 3.336–337 and 15.480–481, and take the same English. κρατί is the dative of κάρα ‘head’ and ἰφθίμῳ ‘mighty’ a stock epithet; κυνέη is a helmet, here εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’. ἵππουριν ‘horse-tailed’, ‘with its horsetail plume’, comes at the start of line 138, parted from its noun by the line division. δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν is ‘fearsomely the crest nodded above’: δεινόν is adverbial, λόφος the plume, and ἔνευεν the imperfect of νεύω ‘nod’.

sentences.t: εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμα δοῦρε, τά οἱ παλάμηφιν ἀρήρει.
sentences.l: And he took two sturdy spears, which to his palm were fitted.
sentences.i: and he took up two sturdy spears that fitted his hand.
sentences.n: Line 3.338 has this line with one spear. εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω ‘took up for himself’. δοῦρε is a dual, ‘two spears’ (δόρυ, plural δοῦρα), and ἄλκιμα ‘sturdy’ agrees with it. τά οἱ παλάμηφιν ἀρήρει: τά is the relative ‘which’, ἀρήρει the pluperfect of ἀραρίσκω ‘be fitted’ with the sense of an imperfect, and παλάμηφιν ‘to his palm’ has the suffix -φιν, which does the work of a preposition and a case.

sentences.t:
ἔγχος δ’ οὐχ ἕλετ’ οἶον ἀμύμονος Αἰακίδαο
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν·
sentences.l:
But the spear alone he did not take of the blameless descendant of Aeacus,
heavy, great, stout;
sentences.i: But the one spear he did not take was that of the blameless descendant of Aeacus, heavy, great and stout;
sentences.n: δέ sets the spear he leaves against the two he takes. οἶον ‘alone’ goes with ἔγχος: the one weapon missing. ἀμύμονος Αἰακίδαο ‘of the blameless descendant of Aeacus’ is Achilles, named by his patronymic as in line 134; ἀμύμων is a stock epithet whose sense is not known. βριθύ ‘heavy’, μέγα ‘great’ and στιβαρόν ‘stout’ stand together in a row without a conjunction, which gives them weight.

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν οὐ δύνατ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν
πάλλειν, ἀλλά μιν οἶος ἐπίστατο πῆλαι Ἀχιλλεὺς
Πηλιάδα μελίην, τὴν πατρὶ φίλῳ πόρε Χείρων
Πηλίου ἐκ κορυφῆς, φόνον ἔμμεναι ἡρώεσσιν.
sentences.l:
this none other of the Achaeans was able
to swing, but Achilles alone knew how to swing it,
the Pelian ash-spear, which to his dear father Chiron gave
from the peak of Pelion, to be slaughter for heroes.
sentences.i: no other of the Achaeans was able to swing it, but Achilles alone knew how to swing it, the Pelian ash-spear that Chiron gave to his dear father from the peak of Pelion, to be the slaughter of heroes.
sentences.n: τὸ μέν ‘this one’ is the spear just left behind, and οὐ δύνατ’ is οὐκ ἐδύνατο ‘could not’, with ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν ‘any other of the Achaeans’. πάλλειν and πῆλαι are two forms of ‘swing, brandish’ (πῆλαι is the aorist infinitive), and the repetition sets all the others against Achilles. μιν is ‘it’, the spear; ἐπίστατο is ‘knew how’. Πηλιάδα μελίην is ‘the Pelian ash’: μελίη is the ash-tree and so the ash-wood spear, and Πηλιάς means ‘of Pelion’, as the mountain is named in the next line. πατρὶ φίλῳ ‘to his dear father’ is Achilles’ father, Peleus, who is not named here. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί, here a purpose infinitive, with φόνον ‘slaughter’ and the dative ἡρώεσσιν ‘for heroes’.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ Αὐτομέδοντα θοῶς ζευγνῦμεν ἄνωγε,
τὸν μετ’ Ἀχιλλῆα ῥηξήνορα τῖε μάλιστα,
πιστότατος δέ οἱ ἔσκε μάχῃ ἔνι μεῖναι ὁμοκλήν.
sentences.l:
And the horses Automedon swiftly to yoke he bade,
him after Achilles the man-breaker he honoured most,
and most trusty to him he was to await in battle the rebuke.
sentences.i: And he bade Automedon yoke the horses swiftly, the man whom, after Achilles the man-breaker, he honoured most, and who was the most trusty to him for standing against a shouted rebuke in battle.
sentences.n: ἄνωγε is a perfect used as a present or past, ‘he bids, he bade’. ζευγνῦμεν is the short infinitive of ζεύγνυμι ‘yoke’, with the ending -μεν for Attic -ναι. Αὐτομέδοντα is the object of ἄνωγε and the subject of the infinitive, and τόν ‘whom’ opens a relative clause that ends with line 146. μετ’ Ἀχιλλῆα ‘after Achilles’ is μετά with the accusative, next in rank; ῥηξήνορα ‘man-breaker’ is Achilles’ stock epithet, and whether it is ranks or men that he breaks is not known. τῖε is the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’, with no augment; ἔσκε is an old form of ἦν ‘was’. μεῖναι ‘to await, to stand against’ takes ὁμοκλήν, a shouted rebuke or threat; the Greek does not say whose, but in battle it is the enemy’s.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ καὶ Αὐτομέδων ὕπαγε ζυγὸν ὠκέας ἵππους
Ξάνθον καὶ Βαλίον, τὼ ἅμα πνοιῇσι πετέσθην,
τοὺς ἔτεκε Ζεφύρῳ ἀνέμῳ Ἅρπυια Ποδάργη
βοσκομένη λειμῶνι παρὰ ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.l:
And for him Automedon also led under the yoke the swift horses,
Xanthus and Balius, the two that with the blasts flew together,
whom she bore to the wind Zephyrus, the Harpy Podarge,
grazing in a meadow beside the stream of Oceanus.
sentences.i: And for him Automedon also led the swift horses under the yoke, Xanthus and Balius, the pair that flew together with the blasts, whom the Harpy Podarge bore to the West Wind as she grazed in a meadow beside the stream of Oceanus.
sentences.n: τῷ δὲ καί: τῷ is ‘for him’, Patroclus, and καί ‘also’ adds the horses to the arming. ὕπαγε ζυγόν is ‘led under the yoke’, ζυγόν an accusative of the place led to. Ξάνθος and Βαλίος are horse-names. τὼ is the dual ‘the two’, and πετέσθην a dual of πέτομαι ‘fly’; ἅμα πνοιῇσι ‘together with the blasts’ says they kept pace with the gusts, and the next lines give the reason in their parentage. Ζεφύρῳ is the West Wind, here with ἀνέμῳ ‘wind’ in apposition. Ἅρπυια ‘Harpy’ is a common noun, ‘snatcher’, a storm-spirit, used here as a being with a name, Ποδάργη, which means ‘swift foot’ or ‘white foot’ (ἀργός has both senses). βοσκομένη is the middle participle of βόσκω ‘graze’, and ῥόον is the accusative of ῥόος ‘stream’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ παρηορίῃσιν ἀμύμονα Πήδασον ἵει,
τόν ῥά ποτ’ Ἠετίωνος ἑλὼν πόλιν ἤγαγ’ Ἀχιλλεύς,
ὃς καὶ θνητὸς ἐὼν ἕπεθ’ ἵπποις ἀθανάτοισι.
sentences.l:
And in the traces blameless Pedasus he put in,
whom once, Eëtion’s city having taken, Achilles led away,
who even though mortal followed the immortal horses.
sentences.i: And he put blameless Pedasus in the traces, the horse that Achilles had once led away when he took the city of Eëtion, and who, mortal though he was, followed the immortal horses.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἵει is a tmesis for ἐνίει, the imperfect of ἐνίημι ‘put in’. παρηορίαι are harness-straps, the traces; the exact gear is not certain, and the picture of a side-horse hitched beside the yoked pair comes from the context. Πήδασον is the name of the horse, and ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’, a stock epithet, is translated although it is said of a horse. ἤγαγ’ is ἤγαγε ‘led away’, and ἑλὼν πόλιν Ἠετίωνος ‘having taken the city of Eëtion’ says how Achilles got him. ἐών is ὤν ‘being’; ἕπεθ’ is ἕπετο ‘followed’, and the immortal horses are Xanthus and Balius.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνας δ’ ἄρ’ ἐποιχόμενος θώρηξεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
πάντας ἀνὰ κλισίας σὺν τεύχεσιν·
sentences.l:
And the Myrmidons, going among them, Achilles armed,
all of them, all through the huts, with their armour;
sentences.i: Achilles went among the Myrmidons and armed them all, all through the huts, in their armour;
sentences.n: Μυρμιδόνας is the object of both ἐποιχόμενος ‘going among’ (the participle of ἐποίχομαι) and θώρηξεν ‘armed’ (the aorist of θωρήσσω, with no augment). The Myrmidons are Achilles’ own men. ἀνὰ κλισίας is ‘all through the huts’, ἀνά with the accusative, the κλισίαι being the huts beside the ships; σὺν τεύχεσιν ‘in their armour’ is a dative plural.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ λύκοι ὣς
ὠμοφάγοι, τοῖσίν τε περὶ φρεσὶν ἄσπετος ἀλκή,
οἵ τ’ ἔλαφον κεραὸν μέγαν οὔρεσι δῃώσαντες
δάπτουσιν·
sentences.l:
and they, like wolves,
raw-eating, in whom about the wits is boundless might,
who a great horned deer on the mountains having slain
devour it;
sentences.i: and they were like wolves that eat raw flesh, in whose wits there is boundless might, and who have killed a great horned deer in the mountains and devour it;
sentences.n: A simile begins: οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Myrmidons, with ὣς set after λύκοι ‘like wolves’. ὠμοφάγοι ‘raw-eating’ is a stock epithet of such beasts. τοῖσιν is the article used as a relative ‘in whose’, and the τε, here and in οἵ τ’, marks a general truth about wolves: the verbs are in the present because the simile tells what wolves do. περὶ φρεσίν is ‘about the wits’, with ἄσπετος ‘boundless’ ἀλκή ‘might’. κεραόν is ‘horned’, and οὔρεσι is the dative plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’ with lengthened first syllable. δῃώσαντες is the aorist participle of δηϊόω ‘cut down’ and δάπτουσιν ‘they devour’.

sentences.t: πᾶσιν δὲ παρήϊον αἵματι φοινόν·
sentences.l: and for all of them the cheek with blood is red;
sentences.i: and the cheek of every one of them is red with blood;
sentences.n: The wolves are still the subject. πᾶσιν is a dative of interest ‘for all of them’, and παρήϊον ‘cheek’ is the neuter subject with the verb ‘is’ understood. φοινόν is ‘red’, the colour of blood, agreeing with παρήϊον, and αἵματι is ‘with blood’.

sentences.t:
καί τ’ ἀγεληδὸν ἴασιν ἀπὸ κρήνης μελανύδρου
λάψοντες γλώσσῃσιν ἀραιῇσιν μέλαν ὕδωρ
ἄκρον ἐρευγόμενοι φόνον αἵματος·
sentences.i: and they go in a pack from a dark-watered spring to lap the dark water at its surface with their slender tongues, belching up the gore of blood;
sentences.n: ἴασιν is the third plural of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἀγεληδόν ‘in a herd’ here means a pack. κρήνης μελανύδρου is ‘a dark-watered spring’, and μέλαν ὕδωρ ‘dark water’ in the next line says it again. λάψοντες is a future participle of purpose, ‘in order to lap’; γλώσσῃσιν ἀραιῇσιν is ‘with slender tongues’ (ἀραιός ‘thin, slight’). ἄκρον ‘topmost’ agrees with ὕδωρ, so they lap the top of the water; it could also be taken as an adverb, and the sense comes out the same. ἐρευγόμενοι is ‘belching up’, and φόνον αἵματος ‘the gore of blood’ is the clotted blood of the kill.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ τε θυμὸς
στήθεσιν ἄτρομός ἐστι, περιστένεται δέ τε γαστήρ·
sentences.l:
and the heart within
their chests is untrembling, and the belly is strained all round;
sentences.i: and the heart in their chests is untrembling, and their bellies are strained all round.
sentences.n: ἐν … στήθεσιν is the preposition set before the noun with other words between (no tmesis): ‘in the chests’. ἄτρομος ‘untrembling’ is ἀ- + τρέμω, a heart that does not shake. The two τε are the same general-truth τε as before. περιστένεται is a rare verb whose sense is not certain; the parts are περί ‘all round’ and a verb of straining or groaning, and ‘is strained all round’ is a guess from the picture of a belly full of meat. θυμός is ‘heart, spirit’, γαστήρ ‘belly’.

sentences.t:
τοῖοι Μυρμιδόνων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ἀμφ’ ἀγαθὸν θεράποντα ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
ῥώοντ’·
sentences.i: Such were the leaders and lords of the Myrmidons as they rushed about the good attendant of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.n: τοῖοι ‘such’ answers the simile: the Myrmidon chiefs were like those wolves. ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες ‘leaders and lords’ is a pair found before, at 2.79. The θεράπων ‘attendant’ is Patroclus, not named but pointed to by his master’s stock epithet ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο ‘of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus’. ῥώοντ’ is ῥώοντο, the imperfect middle of ῥώομαι ‘move quickly, rush’, elided; the ano teleia after it ends the unit before the next clause, which starts in the same line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα τοῖσιν ἀρήϊος ἵστατ’ Ἀχιλλεύς,
ὀτρύνων ἵππους τε καὶ ἀνέρας ἀσπιδιώτας.
sentences.l:
and among them stood warlike Achilles,
urging on both horses and shield-bearing men.
sentences.i: and among them stood warlike Achilles, urging on both horses and shield-bearing men.
sentences.n: ἐν … τοῖσιν is ‘among them’, with ἄρα ‘then’ between. ἵστατ’ is ἵστατο, the imperfect middle of ἵστημι ‘took his stand’. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is a stock epithet of Achilles. ὀτρύνων is ‘urging on’; ἀνέρας is the epic accusative plural of ἀνήρ (Attic ἄνδρας), and ἀσπιδιώτας ‘shield-bearing’ is its stock epithet.

sentences.t:
πεντήκοντ’ ἦσαν νῆες θοαί, ᾗσιν Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐς Τροίην ἡγεῖτο Διῒ φίλος·
sentences.l:
Fifty there were swift ships, in which Achilles
to Troy led, dear to Zeus;
sentences.i: There were fifty swift ships in which Achilles, dear to Zeus, led the way to Troy;
sentences.n: πεντήκοντ’ is elided and stands first for emphasis; νῆες θοαί ‘swift ships’ is a stock phrase. ᾗσιν is the epic dative plural of the relative, ‘in which’. ἡγεῖτο is the imperfect of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, and the Greek gives it no object, so he led the way to Troy. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is a stock epithet; the diaeresis on Διῒ marks the last ι as a syllable of its own. A new paragraph begins here: the catalogue of the Myrmidon force.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῃ
πεντήκοντ’ ἔσαν ἄνδρες ἐπὶ κληῗσιν ἑταῖροι·
sentences.l:
and in each
fifty were the men on the benches, companions;
sentences.i: and in each there were fifty men on the benches, companions.
sentences.n: ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῃ is ‘and in each’ (ship understood), and the unit begins in the middle of line 169. ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’. κληῗσιν is the dative plural of κληΐς, here the thwarts or rowing-benches (the word also means bolt or hook, as the glossary lists), and the diaeresis marks three syllables. ἑταῖροι ‘companions’ is an addition at the end of the line: the fifty men in each ship are Achilles’ followers.

sentences.t:
πέντε δ’ ἄρ’ ἡγεμόνας ποιήσατο τοῖς ἐπεποίθει
σημαίνειν·
sentences.l:
And five then leaders he made, whom he trusted
to give orders;
sentences.i: He made five leaders, whom he trusted to give orders;
sentences.n: ποιήσατο is the aorist middle of ποιέω, ‘made for himself’, appointed. τοῖς ἐπεποίθει is the relative ‘whom’ (τοῖς is the article used as a relative) and the pluperfect of πείθομαι, which has the sense of an imperfect, ‘he trusted’. σημαίνειν is literally ‘to give a sign’ and so ‘to give orders’. The ano teleia after σημαίνειν falls at the beginning of line 172.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δὲ μέγα κρατέων ἤνασσε.
sentences.l: and himself, greatly ruling, was lord.
sentences.i: and he himself, ruling mightily, was lord.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ sets Achilles against the five he has appointed, and the unit begins in the middle of line 172. μέγα κρατέων is ‘ruling mightily’ (κρατέω ‘be strong, hold sway’, with μέγα as an adverb), and ἤνασσε is the imperfect of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’, with the augment. The two verbs say one thing: he alone holds the command.

sentences.t:
τῆς μὲν ἰῆς στιχὸς ἦρχε Μενέσθιος αἰολοθώρηξ
υἱὸς Σπερχειοῖο διιπετέος ποταμοῖο·
sentences.l:
Of the one rank, on the one hand, was leader Menesthius of the glancing breastplate,
son of Spercheius, the Zeus-fallen river;
sentences.i: Of the first rank Menesthius of the glancing breastplate was leader, son of Spercheius, the river fallen from Zeus;
sentences.n: Five ranks are listed, this one and four more (τῆς δ’ ἑτέρης, τῆς δὲ τρίτης, and so on). τῆς … ἰῆς στιχός is a genitive after ἦρχε ‘was leader of’ (ἄρχω with the genitive); ἰῆς is the feminine genitive of ἴα ‘one’ (Attic μιᾶς), and στιχός is ‘rank’. αἰολοθώρηξ is ‘with a glancing breastplate’ (αἰόλος ‘glancing’ + θώρηξ ‘breastplate’), an epithet. Σπερχειοῖο is the genitive of the river Spercheius, and ποταμοῖο ‘river’ stands with it. διιπετέος is a standing epithet of rivers, ‘fallen from Zeus’; the meaning is not certain, and the old gloss is ‘fed by rain’.

sentences.t:
ὃν τέκε Πηλῆος θυγάτηρ καλὴ Πολυδώρη
Σπερχειῷ ἀκάμαντι γυνὴ θεῷ εὐνηθεῖσα,
αὐτὰρ ἐπίκλησιν Βώρῳ Περιήρεος υἷι,
ὅς ῥ’ ἀναφανδὸν ὄπυιε πορὼν ἀπερείσια ἕδνα.
sentences.l:
whom bore Peleus’ daughter, fair Polydora,
to Spercheius, the untiring, a woman who had lain with a god,
but by name to Borus, son of Perieres,
who openly married her, having given unstinted bridal gifts.
sentences.i: whom Peleus’ daughter, fair Polydora, bore to the untiring Spercheius, a woman who had lain with a god, but in name to Borus, son of Perieres, who openly married her after giving unstinted bridal gifts.
sentences.n: ὅν ‘whom’ is Menesthius, the object of τέκε (the aorist of τίκτω, with no augment); Πηλῆος θυγάτηρ is ‘Peleus’ daughter’, Polydora. Σπερχειῷ ἀκάμαντι is ‘to the untiring Spercheius’ (ἀκάμας, ἀ- + κάμνω), and θεῷ is the god she lay with, εὐνηθεῖσα being the aorist passive participle of εὐνάω; so the god is the river. ἐπίκλησιν is an adverbial accusative, ‘by name, in name’: the boy is called the son of Borus, who married her, though his father was the river. ὄπυιε is the imperfect of ὀπυίω ‘take as wife’, said of the man; ἀναφανδόν is ‘openly’, set against the god’s union; πορών is the aorist participle of πόρον ‘gave’. ἀπερείσια ἕδνα ‘unstinted bridal gifts’ are what a suitor gives the bride’s family, and ῥ’ is ῥα ‘indeed’.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ ἑτέρης Εὔδωρος ἀρήϊος ἡγεμόνευε
παρθένιος, τὸν ἔτικτε χορῷ καλὴ Πολυμήλη
Φύλαντος θυγάτηρ·
sentences.i: Of the second rank warlike Eudorus was leader, the son of a maiden, whom Polymele bore, fair in the dance, the daughter of Phylas;
sentences.n: ἑτέρης ‘other’ is here the second rank, after ἰῆς. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is a stock epithet. παρθένιος is ‘son of a maiden’ (παρθένος ‘maiden’), and the lines after explain it. χορῷ καλή is ‘fair in the dance’, χορῷ a dative of respect; Πολυμήλη is Polymele. Φύλαντος is the genitive of Φύλας, whose nominative appears at line 191. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 181.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ κρατὺς ἀργεϊφόντης
ἠράσατ’, ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδὼν μετὰ μελπομένῃσιν
ἐν χορῷ Ἀρτέμιδος χρυσηλακάτου κελαδεινῆς.
sentences.l:
and of her the strong Argeïphontes
fell in love, having seen her with his eyes among the celebrating women
in the dancing-ground of Artemis of the golden distaff, the resounding.
sentences.i: and the strong slayer of Argus fell in love with her, when he saw her among the women celebrating in the dance of Artemis of the golden distaff, the resounding.
sentences.n: τῆς is the genitive after ἠράσατ’ ‘fell in love with’ (the aorist of ἐράομαι, which takes the genitive of the person loved). κρατύς ‘strong’ goes with ἀργεϊφόντης, the epithet used for Hermes (named at line 185); its meaning is disputed, and ‘the slayer of Argus’ is only the traditional gloss. ἰδών is ‘having seen’, ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘with the eyes’. μετὰ μελπομένῃσιν is ‘among those celebrating’, a feminine participle of μέλπω ‘celebrate with song and dance’. χορός is both the dance and the place where it is danced. χρυσηλακάτου ‘of the golden distaff’ is a stock epithet of Artemis (ἠλακάτη ‘distaff’); κελαδεινῆς ‘resounding’ is from κελαδέω ‘make a loud noise’, and what the sound is is not said.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβὰς παρελέξατο λάθρῃ
Ἑρμείας ἀκάκητα, πόρεν δέ οἱ ἀγλαὸν υἱὸν
Εὔδωρον πέρι μὲν θείειν ταχὺν ἠδὲ μαχητήν.
sentences.l:
At once, up into the upper rooms having gone, he lay with her secretly,
Hermes, Akakêta, and gave her a splendid son,
Eudorus, exceedingly swift at running, and a fighter.
sentences.i: At once he went up into the upper rooms and lay with her in secret, Hermes the Harmless, and gave her a splendid son, Eudorus, exceedingly swift at running, and a fighter.
sentences.n: The god of line 181 is named here: Ἑρμείας is the Ionic nominative of Ἑρμῆς. ἀναβάς ‘having gone up’ goes with εἰς ὑπερῷ’ (ὑπερῷα ‘upper rooms’). παρελέξατο is the aorist of παραλέγομαι ‘lie beside’, and λάθρῃ is ‘secretly’. ἀκάκητα is a nominative in -α, like ἱππότα, and an epithet of Hermes whose meaning is unknown; the old guess is ‘one who does no harm’ (ἀ- + κακός), which ‘the Harmless’ reflects. πόρεν is the aorist of πόρον ‘gave’ with no augment, and οἱ is ‘to her’. πέρι is ‘exceedingly’, with ταχύν ‘swift’, and θείειν ‘to run’ is an infinitive of respect, ‘in running’; μαχητήν is ‘fighter’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τόν γε μογοστόκος Εἰλείθυια
ἐξάγαγε πρὸ φόως δὲ καὶ ἠελίου ἴδεν αὐγάς,
sentences.l:
But when indeed him the travail-bringing Eileithyia
brought out to the light, and he saw the rays of the sun,
sentences.i: But when Eileithyia, goddess of the travail of birth, had brought him out into the light and he saw the rays of the sun,
sentences.n: A long sentence is cut here at its first pause. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δή begins a time clause, and its main clause comes at line 189 with τὴν μέν. τόν γε is ‘him’, the baby. μογοστόκος ‘bringing travail’ (μόγος ‘toil’ + τόκος ‘birth’) is the epithet of Εἰλείθυια, goddess of childbirth. ἐξάγαγε is ‘brought out’. πρὸ φόως δέ is πρὸ φόωσδε ‘forth to the light’, φόως ‘light’ with the suffix -δε ‘to’, written as two words. ἴδεν is ‘saw’, with no augment, and ἠελίου is the Ionic genitive of ἠέλιος ‘sun’. To see the rays of the sun is to be born; the subject of ἴδεν is the child, not named again.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν Ἐχεκλῆος κρατερὸν μένος Ἀκτορίδαο
ἠγάγετο πρὸς δώματ’, ἐπεὶ πόρε μυρία ἕδνα,
τὸν δ’ ὃ γέρων Φύλας εὖ ἔτρεφεν ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλεν
ἀμφαγαπαζόμενος ὡς εἴ θ’ ἑὸν υἱὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
her, on the one hand, the strong might of Echecles, Actor’s son,
led home to his house, since he gave countless bridal gifts,
but him the old man Phylas reared well and fostered,
welcoming him warmly as if his own son being.
sentences.i: the strong might of Echecles, Actor’s son, took her home to his house, since he had given countless bridal gifts, but the old man Phylas reared him well and fostered him, welcoming him warmly as if he were his own son.
sentences.n: τὴν μέν ‘her’, Polymele, is answered by τὸν δέ ‘him’, the boy, in line 191. κρατερὸν μένος Ἐχεκλῆος is a periphrasis, ‘the strong might of Echecles’, naming a man by his strength (compare ‘the might of Priam’ at 3.105); Ἀκτορίδαο is the patronymic ‘son of Actor’, with the epic ending -αο. ἠγάγετο is the aorist middle of ἄγω, which in the middle means ‘take home as a wife’; πόρε is ‘gave’, and μυρία ἕδνα ‘countless bridal gifts’. ὁ γέρων Φύλας is ‘the old man Phylas’, the girl’s father named at 181, ὁ being the article. ἔτρεφεν and ἀτίταλλεν are imperfects ‘reared’ and ‘fostered’. ἀμφαγαπαζόμενος is ‘welcoming warmly’. ἑόν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and ἐόντα (Attic ὄντα) agrees with υἱόν, ‘as if he were his own son’.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ τρίτης Πείσανδρος ἀρήϊος ἡγεμόνευε
Μαιμαλίδης, ὃς πᾶσι μετέπρεπε Μυρμιδόνεσσιν
ἔγχεϊ μάρνασθαι μετὰ Πηλεΐωνος ἑταῖρον.
sentences.l:
And of the third Peisander, warlike, was leader,
son of Maemalus, who among all the Myrmidons was conspicuous
at fighting with the spear, after the companion of Peleus’ son.
sentences.i: Of the third rank warlike Peisander, son of Maemalus, was leader, who was conspicuous among all the Myrmidons for fighting with the spear, after the companion of the son of Peleus.
sentences.n: Μαιμαλίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Maemalus’. ὃς … μετέπρεπε is ‘who was conspicuous among’ (μεταπρέπω with the dative πᾶσι Μυρμιδόνεσσιν); ἔγχεϊ μάρνασθαι is an infinitive of respect, ‘in fighting with the spear’. μετά with the accusative ἑταῖρον means ‘after’ in rank: the companion of the son of Peleus (Πηλεΐων, Achilles) is Patroclus, who is first at the spear, and Peisander next. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is again the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
τῆς δὲ τετάρτης ἦρχε γέρων ἱππηλάτα Φοῖνιξ,
πέμπτης δ’ Ἀλκιμέδων Λαέρκεος υἱὸς ἀμύμων.
sentences.l:
And of the fourth was leader the old man, horse-driver Phoenix,
and of the fifth Alcimedon, son of Laerces, blameless.
sentences.i: Phoenix, the old horse-driver, led the fourth rank, and the fifth Alcimedon, the blameless son of Laerces.
sentences.n: The fourth and fifth ranks follow in one sentence. In πέμπτης δ’ Ἀλκιμέδων … there is no verb: ἦρχε is carried over from the line before. γέρων ἱππηλάτα is the stock phrase ‘old horse-driver’ (ἵππος + ἐλαύνω ‘drive’), here with Φοῖνιξ. ἀμύμων ‘blameless’, a stock epithet whose sense is not known, stands at the end for Alcimedon, and Λαέρκεος is the epic genitive of Λαέρκης.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντας ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν Ἀχιλλεὺς
στῆσεν ἐῢ κρίνας, κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε·
sentences.l:
But when all together with the leaders Achilles
had set them up, having sorted them well, and a strong word enjoined on them:
sentences.i: But when Achilles had set all of them up together with their leaders, having sorted them well, he laid a strong charge on them:
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ δή begins a time clause with στῆσεν ‘made stand, set up’ (the transitive aorist of ἵστημι), πάντας ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν ‘all of them together with their leaders’. ἐῢ κρίνας is ‘having sorted well’, κρίνω ‘separate, sort’. κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε has a tmesis, ἐπέτελλε ‘enjoined’, and the whole phrase is the formula of 1.25: a strong word is laid on the hearers, and the speech follows.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνες μή τίς μοι ἀπειλάων λελαθέσθω,
ἃς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν ἀπειλεῖτε Τρώεσσι
πάνθ’ ὑπὸ μηνιθμόν, καί μ’ ᾐτιάασθε ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
“Myrmidons, let no one, for me, forget the threats
which at the swift ships you were threatening against the Trojans
all the while under the wrath, and were blaming me, each one:
sentences.i: “Myrmidons, let none of you forget, I ask, the threats that you kept making against the Trojans at the swift ships all through the time of my wrath, and each of you blamed me:
sentences.n: Μυρμιδόνες is a vocative. μή … λελαθέσθω is a prohibition in the third person, with the aorist imperative middle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’ and the genitive ἀπειλάων (epic genitive plural of ἀπειλή ‘threat’) for the thing forgotten. μοι is an ethic dative, ‘I ask it of you’. ἃς … ἀπειλεῖτε is ‘which you were threatening’ (imperfect), with Τρώεσσι ‘against the Trojans’. πάνθ’ ὑπὸ μηνιθμόν: πάντα is adverbial ‘all the while’, and ὑπό with the accusative marks the time ‘under’ the wrath, that is, during it; the wrath is his own. ᾐτιάασθε is the imperfect of αἰτιάομαι ‘blame’, uncontracted, with ἕκαστος ‘each’ in apposition to ‘you’. The ano teleia ends the unit; the Myrmidons’ words, quoted next, run to line 206.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιε Πηλέος υἱὲ χόλῳ ἄρα σ’ ἔτρεφε μήτηρ,
νηλεές, ὃς παρὰ νηυσὶν ἔχεις ἀέκοντας ἑταίρους·
sentences.l:
‘Cruel one, son of Peleus, on anger, it seems, your mother reared you,
pitiless one, who beside the ships keep your companions unwilling:
sentences.i: ‘Cruel one, son of Peleus, it must have been on anger that your mother reared you, pitiless one, who keep your unwilling companions beside the ships:
sentences.n: Achilles quotes what the Myrmidons used to say, so the English puts single quotation marks inside the double ones, and the quotation runs on to the end of line 206. σχέτλιε is the vocative of σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’, a harsh form of address. χόλῳ ‘on anger’ is a dative of what she nourished him with; χόλος means both bile and anger, and ἄρα marks the conclusion ‘so it must have been’. ἔτρεφε is the imperfect of τρέφω ‘rear’. νηλεές ‘pitiless’ is νηλεής, and ὃς … ἔχεις ‘you who keep’ takes ἀέκοντας ‘unwilling’ (Attic ἄκοντας) ἑταίρους ‘companions’. The grievance is that he holds the men idle by the ships against their will.
sentences.mark: The Myrmidons speak, as Achilles recalls it

sentences.t:
οἴκαδέ περ σὺν νηυσὶ νεώμεθα ποντοπόροισιν
αὖτις, ἐπεί ῥά τοι ὧδε κακὸς χόλος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
Let us go home at least, with our sea-crossing ships,
again, since indeed so evil an anger has fallen upon your heart.’
sentences.i: Let us at least go home again in our sea-crossing ships, since so evil an anger has fallen upon your heart.’
sentences.n: The Myrmidons’ words go on. νεώμεθα is a subjunctive used as an exhortation, ‘let us go’ (νέομαι ‘go back’); περ is ‘at least’, οἴκαδε ‘home’ (-δε marks direction), and αὖτις ‘again, back’ (Attic αὖθις). ἐπεί ῥά τοι is ‘since indeed, to you’, τοι being σοι; ὧδε ‘so’, κακὸς χόλος ‘evil anger’. ἔμπεσε is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fell upon’, the verb used at line 113 for the fire falling on the ships. The inner quotation closes at the end of this line.

sentences.t: ταῦτά μ’ ἀγειρόμενοι θάμ’ ἐβάζετε·
sentences.l: These things to me, gathering, often you were saying;
sentences.i: You used to say these things to me, often, when you gathered together;
sentences.n: Achilles turns from the quoted words to say they were spoken. ταῦτα ‘these things’ looks back; μ’ is μοι ‘to me’, elided. ἀγειρόμενοι is the middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, said of men crowding into groups, and θάμ’ is θαμά ‘often’. ἐβάζετε is the imperfect of βάζω ‘say’, ‘you kept saying’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ πέφανται
φυλόπιδος μέγα ἔργον, ἕης τὸ πρίν γ’ ἐράασθε.
sentences.l:
but now has appeared
the great work of battle-din, which before this you longed for.
sentences.i: but now the great work of the din of battle has appeared, for which you longed before.
sentences.n: πέφανται is the perfect passive of φαίνω, ‘has shown itself, has appeared’. φυλόπιδος is the genitive of φύλοπις ‘the din of battle’, depending on ἔργον, so ‘the great work of battle-din’, the real business of war. ἕης is the epic genitive of the relative ἥ (Attic ἧς), ‘of which’, governed by ἐράασθε, the imperfect of ἐράομαι ‘long for’ (with the genitive), uncontracted; it is not the possessive ἑός ‘his own’. τὸ πρίν γ’ is ‘before now’, with γε stressing it.

sentences.t: ἔνθά τις ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ἔχων Τρώεσσι μαχέσθω.
sentences.l: There let each, a sturdy heart having, fight the Trojans.”
sentences.i: There let each man, keeping a sturdy heart, fight the Trojans.”
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, at the place where the work has now shown itself, the ships. τις is indefinite and in a command means ‘each one’. ἄλκιμον ἦτορ is ‘a sturdy heart’ (ἄλκιμος ‘sturdy’, as in line 139), and ἔχων is ‘keeping’. μαχέσθω is the imperative of μάχομαι, ‘let him fight’, with the dative Τρώεσσι. The speech ends here.
